Missa solemnis. Ludwig van Beethoven's Missa solemnis in D major, Op. 123, completed in 1823, is a monumental setting of the Catholic Mass ordinary. Composed during his late period alongside the Ninth Symphony, it represents one of his most profound, complex, and demanding compositions. Beethoven intended it for the installation of his patron and pupil Archduke Rudolf of Austria as the Archbishop of Olomouc, though its massive scale and length delayed its completion past the ceremony.

The work is marked by its intense vocal difficulty and stands as a deeply personal and dramatic statement of faith. Beethoven inscribed the work with the words "From the heart—may it go again to the heart." The vocal demands on the chorus are notoriously high, requiring singers to sustain extremely high pitches at loud volumes for long durations, similar to the vocal challenges of the Ninth Symphony.

The Benedictus contains a famous, exceptionally long and expressive violin solo that plays alongside the vocalists. This solo symbolizes the Holy Spirit descending to earth. The Kyrie, Gloria, Credo, Sanctus, and Agnus Dei comprise the five traditional divisions of the Latin Mass ordinary that structure the work.

The Agnus Dei concludes with the prayer Dona nobis pacem, which means "Grant us peace." This prayer is dramatically interrupted by distant drum rolls and trumpet fanfares, depicting the terrors of war and contrasting them with a prayer for inner and outer peace. Through these musical contrasts, Beethoven expresses his deepest spiritual convictions.

Archduke Rudolf of Austria was Beethoven's aristocratic patron, student, and friend to whom the mass is dedicated. He was a major patron of science and art in Vienna during the early nineteenth century. The Missa solemnis shares the key of D major with Mozart's Requiem—a key associated with sacred majesty—and both works employ massive choral-orchestral architecture. The Missa solemnis stands as a crowning achievement of Beethoven's final creative period.
